_about: The big picture. Seven levers that adapt inference to the load, in the order a request meets them, plus the loop that re-tunes them and a build order for the reader's position. Each lever says what it listens to in the load, how often it changes, what it has bought (with a baseline) and how it depends on its neighbours. Update a lever's status only when the evidence changes.
umbrella: Inference is becoming adaptive. Seven parts of the stack that were set once now follow the task, the load or the system underneath, each on its own clock. Some adapt while serving, some through training, some through code that agents rewrite. The prompt cache and the model tie them together, so changing one means redoing others.

levers.name: Which model answers
levers.question: Does this session need a frontier model, or will a cheaper open one do?
levers.adapts: The model a session is sent to: a small fast open model, a strong open model, or a closed frontier one. Sub-agents can be routed separately.
levers.listens: How hard the first task of the session looks, live load and price on each model, and whether a cache would be lost by switching.
levers.bought: Vendors report 35 to 74% lower cost against their own baselines. An outside index found all six shipped routers beaten on score and cost by some single model; the best cost a third of its pool's top model for 3.9 points less.
levers.connects: Nine-tenths of agent tokens are cached re-reads, and a cache belongs to one model, so routes change only at session start, compaction or sub-agent launch. Research translators now move a cache between open models for a few points of accuracy. Each routed model needs its own drafter and engine.
levers.story: The router leaves this session on the open model it started with. Switching now would mean re-reading all 142,000 tokens, at full price, on a model that has none of them cached.

levers.name: Which machine takes it
levers.question: Which server already holds this session's context?
levers.adapts: The server each request lands on, and when a session is allowed to move.
levers.listens: Where the session's cached context lives, and how many uncached tokens or active streams each server has in flight.
levers.bought: 2.9x input throughput on code generation against round-robin, and nothing on a decode-bound workload. The saturation threshold has to be recalibrated per model and chip.
levers.connects: Sticky routing is what makes the prompt cache pay, and the cache is most of an agent workload's cost. It needs the cache map kept by lever 3, and it can take hints from the agent harness about priority and expected length.
levers.story: It goes back to the server that handled turn 42, because that server still holds the session's history in its cache. A less busy server would have to fetch or recompute all of it.

levers.name: How the cluster is divided
levers.question: How much of the cluster should read prompts, and how much should write answers?
levers.adapts: The share of machines doing prefill against decode, the size of batches, and which cached contexts are kept or evicted.
levers.listens: The mix of long prompts and steady generation, and which contexts agents are still waiting to reuse.
levers.bought: 1.28x over the best fixed split as traffic shifts, in research. A prefill cap: up to 93% more tokens per GPU-second. A host-memory cache tier: 3.9x once sessions outgrew the GPU. A shared cache store cut one provider's prefill nodes from 58 to 34.
levers.connects: It decides how full batches are, which sets how much speculation (lever 4) is worth and which shapes the kernels (lever 5) see. Evicting the wrong context undoes lever 2. Splitting prefill from decode left one provider drafting tokens decode never used.
levers.story: Only the new part needs reading, so the machines that read prompts barely notice. What matters is whether turn 42's history is still in GPU memory, in host memory, or gone.

levers.name: How tokens get written
levers.question: How far ahead can a cheap draft guess before the big model has to check?
levers.adapts: The draft model, how many tokens it guesses ahead for this request, and whether to speculate at all at the current load. The drafter itself can keep training on live traffic.
levers.listens: How predictable the output is in this domain (code and maths speculate well, chat does not), how full the batches are right now, and how many recent guesses were accepted.
levers.bought: About 3x for one request, 1 to 1.5x at 32 concurrent; on a large mixture-of-experts model the recipe setting lost from 16. A load-aware scheduler raised throughput by half. Draft length by batch size added up to 15%. A self-training drafter adds 1.25x.
levers.connects: A drafter fits one model and quantisation: tune or swap the model (levers 1 and 6) and it is rebuilt. One analysis says mixture-of-experts models pay most at small batches; one measurement shows the usual fade. Checking competes with real requests for batch room, so tune with lever 3.
levers.story: A small draft model guesses several tokens ahead and the big model checks them in one pass. Code is predictable, so most guesses land. If the batch is full, the scheduler guesses fewer.

levers.name: How the engine runs it
levers.question: What are the fastest kernels and settings for this model, on this chip, under this traffic?
levers.adapts: The kernels, how operations are fused, the parallelism layout and the engine's settings.
levers.listens: Batch sizes, sequence lengths, cache-hit rates, and which parts of the model real inputs actually exercise.
levers.bought: 43% more throughput under a per-user speed floor against the best published run. Merged agent-written kernels: 1.3 to 1.9x on decode. Kernel gains measured alone mostly vanish end to end. Fused decode chosen per step: 1.2 to 2.3x for one user, fading with load.
levers.connects: This is where agent loops do most of their work today. Every lever above changes the shapes this one sees, so re-tuning any of them can undo it. It is redone for each new model and each new chip.
levers.story: Every step runs kernels tuned for this model on this chip, some written by coding agents and merged upstream, with settings chosen for agent traffic: long prompts, short answers.

levers.name: What the model is
levers.hint: under every step above: the weights themselves, tuned to a domain or retrained from live use
levers.question: Could a smaller model, trained on this domain, do the job a bigger general one does now?
levers.adapts: The weights: reinforcement learning or fine-tuning on a customer's tasks, code and tool formats, retraining from live use, distilling a frontier model into a small one, and how hard they are quantised.
levers.listens: The domain's tasks and tool-calling format, logged production outputs to learn from, and where the general model fails or is slower than it needs to be.
levers.bought: In production: a coding model retrained from live use every five hours kept 2.3% more edits; a company-tuned model kept 17% more code; a daily-retrained small model replaced a frontier one at an estimated 96% less. Tunes go stale within months.
levers.connects: A tuned model lets lever 1 send more sessions down the cheap path. It needs its own drafter (lever 4) and compiled engine (lever 5), and it dies when its base model is withdrawn. General models passed one tune within three months. Adapters sharing one deployment keep it affordable.
levers.story: Under all of it sits the model itself. If the product retrains it from live use, as one does every five hours, or the provider keeps training its drafter on this traffic, part of the fit happened before the request arrived.

levers.name: How deep each token goes
levers.question: Should this token run part of the model again, given how hard it is and how busy the machine is?
levers.adapts: How many passes a looped model makes through its shared middle layers, fixed at release today and per token where a model allows it, or where a token exits early. Weights stay the same.
levers.listens: How sure the model already is of the next token, how full the batches are, the request's latency budget, and how much cache memory each extra pass would take.
levers.bought: Trained in, loops let one lab ship a 26B it says leads open models under 100B on coding, and a second pass on 7% of tokens adds 3 to 4 points. Retrofitted, a point or two; a plain 14B beat a looped 8B.
levers.connects: Extra passes compete for batch room like speculation (lever 4), and the window and step count are found per model like engine settings (lever 5). Trained loops keep a cache per pass over the prompt, so more passes mean fewer sequences per GPU. Training-free loops keep the cache size.
levers.story: On a looped model, an easy token takes one pass through the shared middle layers and a hard one takes another. Most models in production run a fixed depth today.

loop.name: The loop
loop.hint: agents and a measuring rig re-tune every lever as the load changes
loop.text: None of the seven levers is new. What changed in 2026 is the cost of re-tuning them. Coding agents, pointed at a rig that replays real traffic and measures end to end, now do in a day what took a performance engineer a month, and can do it again when the model, the chip or the traffic changes.
loop.connects: Today the loop works mostly on lever 5, a little on levers 3 and 4, and has only begun on 1 and 6 (one company had an agent run its fine-tuning). Its limit is not the agent but the rig: knowing whether a change is real.
loop.story: Overnight, agents replay traffic like this against candidate kernels and settings, and keep only what measures faster end to end. A person approves what ships, so tomorrow's request meets a slightly different stack.

build_intro: Written for a provider serving many models. The order follows where others report the most gain for the least new code. Steps 4 to 7 repeat for every model, so do them for the few that carry most of your traffic and rely on the open engines for the rest. It is drawn from published accounts, not from a system anyone has documented end to end.

build.name: Record your traffic and learn to replay it
build.do: Capture real sessions at your gateway with their timing, context lengths and cache behaviour, strip the content, and replay them against a candidate stack at real concurrency. Replayers exist; the capture and redaction side you write yourself.
build.bought: Nothing by itself. It let an academic group with no customers top the public board, and drives one company's loop. Public agent traces overstated capacity by about 1.7x for four models and hid a routing bug.
build.watch: Mean traces overstate throughput by 10 to 20%, reruns hit a warm cache, and traces from another model mislead. One provider's stored prompts leaked through an agent-committed credential; it now defaults new accounts to zero retention.

parts.label: AIPerf trace replay
parts.note: NVIDIA. Replays recorded agent sessions with their timing and shared prefixes against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

parts.label: AgentX harness
parts.note: The public benchmark's own replayer, a fork of AIPerf, with 393 coding-agent traces.

parts.label: TraceLab
parts.note: University of Washington. Collects and sanitises agent session logs: sizes and timing, no content.

parts.label: trie
parts.note: Applied Compute. Under 1,000 lines; replays sessions by shape and reports cache-hit rates.

parts.label: TensorRT-LLM trace replay
parts.note: Adds jobs per hour, and computes the best achievable cache-hit rate without a GPU.

build.name: Add gates that catch a fake win
build.do: Measure every change end to end inside the full engine, never a kernel alone. Check outputs in three layers: kernel tests across shapes, a token-probability comparison, and task evals that exercise the changed path. Fail on request errors.
build.bought: Protection. Kernel speed-ups of 1.6 to 6.6x shrank to about 1x end to end, and one in sixteen agent runs in an independent benchmark gamed the measurement.
build.watch: A standard task-score gate caught 1 of 7 known numerical bugs. Agents have been caught changing the benchmark. An upstream fused kernel shipped that garbled about one long code reply in nine.

parts.label: vLLM fast-track RFC
parts.note: The evidence an agent-written optimisation must carry: isolation, end-to-end evals, kernel tests, no regression above 1%.

parts.label: vLLM bring-your-own-GPU evals RFC
parts.note: Task tolerances calibrated from repeated runs, plus a token-probability check.

parts.label: SGLang agent skills
parts.note: Includes a test comparing each token's probability on the prefill and decode paths.

parts.label: klgate
parts.note: A prototype of the probability check with a permutation test in place of a fixed threshold.

build.name: Tune what needs no new code
build.do: Search the settings you already have against the rig: cache-aware and sticky routing, the prefill and decode split, caps on long prefills, cache retention. Use plain search here, not agents. Screen candidates in a simulator first: one picked policies that held on hardware.
build.bought: The largest reported gains for the least risk: 2.9x from cache-aware routing on code generation, 3.9x from a host-memory cache tier once sessions outgrew GPU memory, up to 93% from a prefill cap. One default flag explained 78% of a gap between two engines.
build.watch: Plain search beat every coding agent here in an independent test. Prefill-bound gains do not appear on decode-bound work. A shared-storage cache tier added 14 to 66% to first-token time and paid only on failover.

parts.label: llm-d
parts.note: Cache-aware and load-aware routing on Kubernetes over vLLM and SGLang, with a latency predictor that retrains on live traffic.

parts.label: NVIDIA Dynamo
parts.note: Routing by cached-prefix overlap, hints from the agent harness, and a planner that forecasts load.

parts.label: DynoSim
parts.note: Simulates scheduling and caching without GPUs to shortlist settings. Confirm the shortlist on real hardware.

parts.label: BLIS
parts.note: A simulator of the serving pipeline that runs on CPUs. 6.7% median error against real runs, and two policies found in it were merged into llm-d. For scheduling and admission, not engine code.

build.name: Fit the decoding to the traffic
build.do: Measure how well your traffic speculates, by domain, by load and by model, before building anything. Train a draft model for each target model, and let the draft length follow the live batch size, down to zero.
build.bought: About 3x for a single request, 1 to 1.5x at 32 concurrent. A load-aware scheduler with a new drafter: about half more live throughput. Draft length by batch size alone: up to 15%. Tuning the drafter to the workload: 20 to 45%.
build.watch: Under load some drafters fall below break-even; the engines' recipe for one mixture-of-experts model lost from 16 concurrent. A purpose-trained drafter only matched the shipped one in an outside test. Rebuild it whenever the model changes.

parts.label: Speculators
parts.note: vLLM project and Red Hat. Trains draft models from a running server's hidden states and serves them directly.

parts.label: SPEED-Bench
parts.note: Measures acceptance across 11 kinds of content, and throughput under load, inside production engines.

parts.label: Aurora
parts.note: Together's open-source drafter that keeps training on live traffic.

parts.label: inference-lab
parts.note: Doubleword, MIT licence. Simulates a vLLM-shaped engine so a draft-length policy can be priced before it is built. Its figures are upper bounds until calibrated against a real engine.

build.name: Automate bringing up each new model
build.do: Have an agent port each new model into your engine against an exact oracle: its outputs must match the reference layer by layer. Then run steps 3 and 4 for it from a script, not by hand.
build.bought: On the public board, a new model's throughput per GPU rose 1.2 to 2.9x per chip in its first fortnight. Published skills let a coding agent port a model by chasing layer-by-layer divergence. A typical start-up changes its top model within a month.
build.watch: Bring-up times show on the public board; no provider has published its own time or cost. Porting has an exact oracle and optimisation does not, so the gate for one will not do for the other.

parts.label: Modular agent skills
parts.note: Two published skills for porting a model: scaffold from the nearest architecture, then hunt divergence against the reference.

parts.label: MetaInfer
parts.note: Skills for porting models to less common accelerators, with a correctness gate that runs first.

parts.label: SGLang agent skills
parts.note: Includes consistency tests between the prefill and decode paths, useful as a bring-up check.

build.name: Point agents at the engine
build.do: Give coding agents the rig, an engine that reloads code in seconds, and a plain goal. Start with the models that carry most of your traffic, and let short profiles of live deployments pick the targets. People review the evidence and approve what ships.
build.bought: 43% under a speed floor in three days; merged kernels worth 1.3 to 1.9x on decode; a whole bespoke engine in a week for about 200 GPU-hours; across a hyperscaler's fleet, 3 to 6% per fix on 50 to 100 deployments.
build.watch: Curated knowledge and expert playbooks made one team's agents worse. Review is the queue: patches arrive faster than people can read them.

parts.label: SGLang agent skills
parts.note: 32 published skills: profiling, CUDA debugging, incident replay, consistency tests.

parts.label: Kernel Design Agents
parts.note: NVIDIA Research and MIT. A contract, plan and verify workflow for kernel work.

parts.label: MetaInfer
parts.note: A skills-only toolkit with a correctness gate that runs before profiling. One provider built a custom engine with it.

build.name: Choose between models, and tune one where the job is narrow
build.do: Start from the best single model for the job and route only where the work is varied, deciding at session start or where no cache is lost. Post-train an open model only for single jobs where you have the data and a grader.
build.bought: Routing: 35 to 74% lower cost by vendors' accounts. An outside index found every shipped router beaten on score and cost by a single model; one vendor reports its router ahead on another public board. Tuning: 11 to 21 points on a legal benchmark for four open models.
build.watch: Nobody has tested a router on live sessions with the cache priced. A tune needs its own drafter and engine, has been passed by general models within three months, and dies with its base model.

parts.label: Vals Router Index
parts.note: An outside index that runs routers and single models through the same long agentic tasks. Look a router up here before paying for one.

parts.label: TwinRouterBench
parts.note: Scores a router step by step with prompt caching priced in. Use it before trusting a router.

parts.label: OpenRouter router benchmarks
parts.note: Routers beside single models from the same pool on public tasks. Read it per benchmark, not the averaged chart.

parts.label: Agentic RL recipe
parts.note: An open recipe for reinforcement learning on a large open model: about 64 GPUs for five days.

parts.label: Together Post-Training
parts.note: A hosted trainer where you write the loop. Adapters share one deployment.

parts.label: Fireworks Training API
parts.note: The same shape from another provider. Check its changelog for which base models are still tunable.

build.name: Close the loop
build.do: Detect when traffic has drifted, re-run the earlier steps, promote winners through shadow traffic, and send upstream whatever is not specific to you.
build.bought: One provider shadowed all live traffic onto a new build before cutover. Another screens changes in a calibrated simulator, then live A/B tests, with an engineer approving each. Prompt lengths have been seen to rise about 80% within two weeks of a model release.
build.watch: No provider has published how it detects drift, and nothing public compares a shadow's outputs with the live side. Nobody can yet simulate traffic they have not seen.

parts.label: Gateway API request mirroring
parts.note: Copies live requests to a shadow service and discards its replies. Comparing the two sides is left to you.

parts.label: Dynamo planner
parts.note: Forecasts load and tracks how far observed latency has drifted from the profile.

parts.label: TIDE
parts.note: Research: keeps a drafter aligned with live traffic and turns speculation off when it stops paying.

build_note: Written in-house because nothing public exists: capture and redaction at your gateway, comparing a shadow's outputs and latency with the live side, an engine that reloads candidate code in seconds, and the detector that decides when to re-tune. The cost of the whole thing is also missing from every public account; one figure exists for one step.

open_ground.head: How to tell that traffic has drifted
open_ground.text: Every loop re-tunes when the load changes. No provider has published how it detects that, with what signal, threshold or window. Alibaba sidesteps it, profiling live deployments in 30-second windows for known waste.

open_ground.head: Judging a change on traffic you have not seen
open_ground.text: Replay covers only what was recorded; another model's traces overstated capacity by 1.7x. A simulator picks scheduling policies that hold on hardware. None judges engine or kernel changes or is checked against live traffic.

open_ground.head: Tuning the levers together
open_ground.text: Each lever is tuned alone, yet they are coupled through the cache and the model. Two systems set speculation by load; nobody tunes routing, decoding and the engine jointly.

open_ground.head: What the loop costs per model
open_ground.text: One figure exists: about 200 GPU-hours for one bespoke engine. With many models, cost per model per month decides whether any of this pays.

open_ground.head: Whether gains compound from one cycle to the next
open_ground.text: The recursive claim needs gain per cycle to rise, or a model trained on optimisation traces to beat its teacher. Nobody has shown either.

open_ground.head: Moving a session between models without a re-read
open_ground.text: Three research systems translate a cache between open models for a few points of accuracy. None is in production or crosses a closed model's API, and one was tested on agent tasks.

matrix.intro: Serving used to be set once, by hand, for everyone. Parts of it now adapt to three things: the task being asked, the load on the machines and the system underneath. They adapt in three ways, each on its own clock. Select any square.

to.name: The task
to.desc: Code or chat, easy or hard, which field. Code and maths are easier to predict than chat, and a narrow job can be done by a smaller model.

to.name: The load
to.ask: How busy, and in what shape?
to.desc: How many requests at once, how long the prompts are, and how much of each is already cached. Agent traffic means long prompts, short answers and constant re-reading.

to.name: The system
to.desc: The model's architecture, the chip and the engine. A setting, a kernel or a draft model tuned for one rarely suits another.

by.name: Choose
by.desc: Pick among options that already exist: which model, which machine, how far to guess ahead, how many passes. No weights or code change.

by.name: Train
by.desc: Change the weights. Tune a model for a field, train the draft model on the traffic it serves and swap it in live, or train for the chip it will run on.

by.name: Rewrite
by.desc: Change the code. Coding agents write kernels and engine paths for this model, chip and traffic, and a rig that replays real traffic decides what ships.

cells.head: Route by task, think longer on hard tokens
cells.stat: Extra pass on hard tokens: +3.8 points
cells.text: A router reads the start of a session and picks a cheap open model or a frontier one. A looped model gives a hard token another pass through its middle layers. Speculation pays most on code and maths.
cells.number: A second pass on hard tokens added 3.8 points for 4 to 5% more compute, against a single-pass twin. An outside index found all six shipped routers beaten by a single model.

cells.head: Follow the cache, guess less when busy
cells.text: Each request goes to the server that already holds its history. The cluster moves machines between reading prompts and writing answers as traffic changes. Draft models guess fewer tokens ahead when batches are full.
cells.number: Cache-aware routing gave 2.9x input throughput on code generation, against round-robin. A scheduler that sets speculation by load raised one lab's live throughput by about half.

cells.head: Settings fitted to the model and chip
cells.text: The parallelism layout, batch limits, cache format and draft length all depend on the model's architecture and the chip. A layout that suited one model's attention failed on the next, and speculation pays differently on mixture-of-experts models.
cells.number: On one model, matching a single default setting removed 78% of the largest capacity gap between two open engines, measured by an outside team.

cells.head: Retrain the model on the work it does
cells.stat: Retrained from live use every five hours
cells.text: A product retrains its own model on what users do with it, or tunes a model on one company's code or one field's tasks, and ships new weights behind an A/B test. It must be redone as base models change.
cells.number: Cursor retrains its model from live use as often as every five hours; in an A/B test 2.3% more edits were kept. Google's model tuned on its own code kept 17% more code for 29,000 engineers.

cells.head: Train the draft model on live traffic
cells.text: The small model that guesses tokens ahead is trained on the traffic it actually serves, keeps learning from which guesses were accepted, and is swapped in while the server runs. Here training is part of serving.
cells.number: A drafter trained online from live traffic ran about 1.25x faster than a well-trained static one. Drafters trained on one customer's traffic gave 1.2 to 1.45x over generic ones. All vendor-measured.

cells.head: Train for the model and the chip
cells.text: A draft model is built for one model and must be rebuilt when that model changes. Some models are now trained in the low-precision formats their chips run, with heads that draft their own tokens, and on the serving engine's own kernels.
cells.number: A block drafter accepted 21% more tokens per check than its predecessor, for 1.3% more time per cycle. A trainer running vLLM's serving kernels matched the served model exactly, at 91% of rollout speed.

cells.head: Tune the whole stack to one customer
cells.text: A company points agents at its own traffic, adapting engine settings, kernels and drafters to its one workload. So far tuning to one customer has bought tens of percent; tuning to a whole class of traffic has bought multiples.
cells.number: One customer-service company's agents raised requests per GPU within its latency limit 2.5x over its starting setup; a drafter adapted to its own traffic gave 1.34x. Both self-reported.

cells.head: Rewrite the engine for the traffic shape
cells.text: Agents profile the engine on replayed traffic, write fixes where real requests spend their time, and recompile as traffic drifts. The long prompts and constant re-reading of agent traffic changed which code paths matter.
cells.number: An off-the-shelf coding agent found kernel fixes worth 43% more throughput at 30 tokens a second per user, against the best published run on a public agent benchmark.

cells.head: New kernels for each model and chip
cells.text: Coding agents write kernels and fused decode paths for one model on one chip, build engines for new accelerators, and port each new architecture. Gains measured on a kernel alone mostly shrink to almost nothing inside the full engine.
cells.number: Agent-written kernels merged into vLLM for one model on one chip gave 1.31 to 1.92x decode throughput over the stock engine, from 1 to 64 requests at once.

walk.intro: One agent turn, followed through every decision the stack makes for it, in order. The request is the median of a public set of coding-agent traces.
walk.request: The 43rd turn of a coding agent's session: 142,000 tokens of history, almost all of it read on earlier turns, plus a new tool result. It will write back about 440 tokens.
